summary: Provides a way to negotiate transferring one or more files between two endpoints using the SDP offer/answer model from RFC 3264. SDP is extended to describe the files, and the offerer can describe files it wants to send or receive.

plainLanguage.summary: Before sending a gift, you ask if the other person wants it. This note lets two programs agree on which files to swap before sending them.

questions: how to negotiate file transfer with sdp
what is msrp file transfer in sdp
what is the sdp file-selector attribute
subtitle: How two endpoints use the SDP offer/answer model to agree on a file transfer, with MSRP carrying the bytes.

tldr.problem: Plain MSRP can carry files, but it cannot tell the recipient that a file transfer is coming, let them accept or decline it based on the file's details, or let them ask for a specific file.
tldr.mechanism: SDP gains media-level attributes that describe a file (file-selector, file-transfer-id, file-disposition, file-date, file-icon, file-range). One "m=" line describes one file, the SDP direction attribute says push or pull, and MSRP carries the file after the answerer accepts.
tldr.outcome: Either side can offer to send a file or ask for one, and the answerer accepts or rejects each file separately before any data moves. The RFC recommends integrity protection and encryption for the SDP carrying these attributes.

facts.label: Streams per file
facts.value: One m= line and one MSRP session per file

today: RFC 5547 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Baseline MSRP Is Missing
sections.content:
The SDP offer/answer model of RFC 3264 lets two endpoints agree on a multimedia session. The Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP, RFC 4975) sends messages in the context of a session and can carry arbitrary MIME content such as images or video clips. MSRP also has features useful for files: message chunking shares a connection between a large file and interactive messages without blocking them, relays help with NAT traversal, and S/MIME can protect content.

However, baseline MSRP lacks four things: telling "file transfer" apart from "file attached to an IM"; a request that the recipient can accept or decline before the transfer starts; meta information about the file (at least content type, size, hash, name and a short description); and a way for the recipient to request a file from the sender.
sections.plainLanguage: Plain chat can send a file, but it just shows up. Nobody gets to ask "what is it, and do I want it?" first.

sections.title: Overview: Push, Pull and One File per Line
sections.content:
The offerer builds an SDP body describing one or more files it wants to send or receive. The answerer accepts or rejects each file separately. The file sender is the endpoint willing to send a file and the file receiver is the one willing to take it.

  • In a push operation the offerer is the file sender. The offer contains sendonly and the answer contains recvonly.
  • In a pull operation the offerer is the file receiver. The offer contains recvonly and the answer contains sendonly.

Each SDP m= line describes an MSRP media stream that transfers a single file, so several simultaneous files need several lines. Multiple MSRP sessions can share one transport connection. The actual transfer is plain MSRP once the answerer accepts.

A regular MSRP endpoint that knows nothing of these extensions can in principle still act as answerer and file receiver, but the user experience is reduced because it cannot show the reason for the session or accept or reject by file attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each file gets its own lane. You say "I'll give you this" (push) or "please give me that" (pull), and the other side says yes or no for each lane.

sections.title: The File Selector and Other Attributes
sections.content:
A file selector is a tuple of one or more of four selectors: name, size, type and hash. It lets both sides refer to the same file, and it must end up choosing at most one file. The hash uses SHA-1; a hash alone is usually enough to pin down a single file. Implementations MUST implement file-selector, and offers and answers for file transfer MUST contain it with at least one selector.

The other new media-level attributes are:

  • file-transfer-id: a random, globally unique identifier for the transfer.
  • file-disposition: a hint about whether to render the file or treat it as an attachment.
  • file-date: creation, modification and read dates, at most one of each, in RFC 5322 format with numeric time zones.
  • file-icon: a Content-ID URL pointing to a small preview image.
  • file-range: a start and stop octet, so a transfer can be interrupted and resumed. The first octet is number 1, and the stop offset may be an asterisk when the size is unknown. With no attribute, the whole file is meant, as if the value were 1-*.

The name selector is UTF-8, must not contain characters the local operating system treats as directory structure (those are percent-encoded), and receivers must sanitize it before touching the file system.
sections.plainLanguage: The file selector is a description card: its name, size, kind and a fingerprint. The fingerprint (hash) is the surest way to point at exactly one file.

sections.title: Negotiating, Accepting and Rejecting
sections.content:
An offerer MUST put one m= line per file in the SDP, along with the attributes MSRP itself requires such as a=path and a=accept-types. A file sender adds sendonly and describes the file; a file receiver adds recvonly and at least one selector, and the RFC recommends it include no other file attributes.

The answerer rejects a file by setting that line's port to zero, and the rejecting answer MUST mirror the file-selector and file-transfer-id of the offer. For a push, the answerer typically asks the user, copies any name, type and size selectors into the answer, copies the transfer ID, and adds recvonly. For a pull, the answerer applies the selector to its files: if none match it rejects the stream, and if several match it may choose one by local policy or reject. If it accepts a single match it answers with sendonly and SHOULD add the SHA-1 hash of the whole file.

After the transfer, the receiver SHOULD compute the hash and check the other selectors, and if they do not match it SHOULD treat the transfer as failed and inform the user. If an offer carries a file-range the answerer accepts, it MUST repeat the same range in its answer.

An endpoint can advertise capability by adding an empty file-selector to its m=message line in a capability response.
sections.plainLanguage: Saying no is easy: you just close that file's lane. Saying yes means copying back the details so both sides know they mean the same file, and checking the fingerprint at the end.

sections.title: Transfer IDs, Repeats and Aborts
sections.content:
SDP is often resent for unrelated reasons, for example a SIP session timer refresh with a re-INVITE or adding another media stream. Without help, the other side could not tell whether a repeated file description is a new request. The file-transfer-id solves this: implementations MUST include it in offers and answers, the offerer picks a unique value (a relatively big random one, e.g., 32 characters, is RECOMMENDED), and the answerer copies it.

  • A new ID means a new transfer. A resumed transfer counts as new, so it needs a new ID.
  • An unchanged ID with the same selected file means the existing transfer, which is left alone.
  • An unchanged ID with a different selected file is an error, and the answerer MUST abort.

Sending an otherwise identical offer with a new ID mid-transfer tells the answerer to abort and restart. Either side can abort an ongoing transfer. A sender aborts the MSRP message by putting the hash character in the end-line continuation field of a SEND request, then SHOULD send a new offer with the port set to zero. A receiver whose SEND request carried a Failure-Report other than no answers with an MSRP 413 response and then closes the session with a zero-port offer; if Failure-Report was no, it just sends the zero-port offer.
sections.plainLanguage: Every file handoff gets a ticket number. Same ticket, same file means "we're already on it". A new ticket means "start over".

sections.title: How MSRP Carries the File
sections.content:
Each MSRP session set up this way carries exactly one file, and senders MUST NOT send additional files over it. A file goes in a single MSRP message, though it may be split into chunks, and pipelined SEND requests are valid. Because MSRP treats the whole delivered content as one message, it counts bytes from 1 regardless of position in the file. If a file-range is present, the sender extracts those octets and may wrap them, for instance in the message/cpim wrapper that MSRP implementations must support.

File transfer can happen in a new session or inside an existing one, including one used for ordinary messaging, but the offerer MUST NOT reuse an m= line still in use by MSRP. A receiver may add the MSRP max-size attribute, and senders MUST NOT exceed it. The default disposition for MSRP bodies is render; for files attachment is also possible.

An icon travels in the signaling, so the SDP and the icon must be wrapped in a multipart/related body with the SDP as root. If the far end rejects it for not supporting multipart, the sender is RECOMMENDED to drop the icon and resend plain SDP. Icons should be kept small.
sections.plainLanguage: Each file travels in its own envelope on its own lane, and the receiver can say how big an envelope it will accept.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker who changes the SDP attributes could make a receiver think a different file is coming, or make a sender send the wrong file. The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS integrity protection for SDP carrying these attributes, and that senders verify the file against its selectors. File descriptions may be confidential, so encrypting the SDP is also RECOMMENDED. TLS and S/MIME are named as the natural choices.

The answerer MUST authenticate the offerer and then authorize the transfer, typically through the mechanisms of SIP and MSRP. A misbehaving peer may try to exhaust memory or disk with very large files, so implementations should limit file size, check free space, and limit simultaneous transfers. Receivers MUST sanitize input such as the file name before calling the local file system. Finally, file transfer is a common route for viruses, spyware and other malware, so receivers should apply anti-virus and similar protections.
sections.plainLanguage: Make sure the note describing the file cannot be swapped, only accept files from people you trust, and scan whatever arrives.

data.title: File description in SDP
data.code:
m=message 7654 TCP/MSRP *
i=This is my latest picture
a=sendonly
a=accept-types:message/cpim
a=accept-wrapped-types:*
a=file-selector:name:"My cool picture.jpg" type:image/jpeg
  size:32349 hash:sha-1:
  72:24:5F:E8:65:3D:DA:F3:71:36:2F:86:D4:71:91:3E:E4:A2:CE:2E
a=file-transfer-id:vBnG916bdberum2fFEABR1FR3ExZMUrd
a=file-disposition:attachment
a=file-date:creation:"Mon, 15 May 2006 15:01:31 +0300"
a=file-icon:cid:id2@alicepc.example.com
a=file-range:1-32349
